pages.title: Introduction to Heaps
pages.content:
### Introduction to Heaps
A **heap** is a complete binary tree with a priority rule between every parent and child.

- A **min-heap** keeps each parent less than or equal to its children, so the minimum is at the root.
- A **max-heap** keeps each parent greater than or equal to its children, so the maximum is at the root.
- Heaps are commonly stored in arrays, making them useful for priority queues, scheduling, greedy algorithms, and heap sort.

The root is at index `0`. With zero-based indexing, the children of index `i` are `2*i+1` and `2*i+2`.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Introduction to Heaps: apply the heap invariant and the correct array-index relationships for reliable implementation.

checkpoint.question: What does the root guarantee in a binary heap?
options: A min-heap keeps the minimum at the root and a max-heap keeps the maximum at the root.
The root is always the most recently inserted value.
The root must be the median value.
The root can ignore the heap invariant until deletion.
checkpoint.explanation: The heap invariant guarantees that the root contains the highest-priority value.

pages.title: Representation of binary trees as array
pages.content:
### Array Representation of a Binary Heap
A complete binary tree can be stored level-by-level in a zero-indexed array.

For a node at index `i`:
- left child = `2*i+1`
- right child = `2*i+2`
- parent for `i>0` = `(i-1)/2`

For example, `[2,4,7,8,15,10,18,21]` represents a complete binary tree without storing explicit child pointers. Check child indexes against the array length before accessing them.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Representation of binary trees as array: apply the heap invariant and the correct array-index relationships for reliable implementation.

pages.title: Finding indexes of the children of a node
pages.content:
### Finding Indexes of the Children
In a zero-indexed heap array, the candidate child indexes for a node at index `i` are:

- `left = 2*i + 1`
- `right = 2*i + 2`

For index `6`, the candidates are `13` and `14`. They are valid only when they are smaller than the heap size. This simple arithmetic is the basis of iterative sift-up and sift-down operations.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Finding indexes of the children of a node: apply the heap invariant and the correct array-index relationships for reliable implementation.

pages.title: MCQ about Heaps
pages.content:
### Heap Root and Priority
The root gives the highest-priority value currently stored.

For the values `13, 12, 51, 2, 14, 17, 15`, a min-heap places `2` at the root. The internal arrangement is not required to be fully sorted; only the parent-child heap invariant must hold.

This is why a heap is useful when an application repeatedly needs the smallest or largest item.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: MCQ about Heaps: apply the heap invariant and the correct array-index relationships for reliable implementation.

pages.title: Time Complexity of Heap operations
pages.content:
### Time Complexity of Heap Operations
For a binary heap containing `N` elements:

- `top` is **O(1)** because the root is at index `0`.
- `push` is **O(log N)** in the worst case because a new value may move up the heap.
- `pop` is **O(log N)** in the worst case because a replacement value may move down.
- Bottom-up heap construction is **O(N)**.
- The heap occupies **O(N)** space.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Time Complexity of Heap operations: apply the heap invariant and the correct array-index relationships for reliable implementation.

pages.title: Heap Sort
pages.content:
### Heap Sort
Heap sort can sort an array in **O(N log N)** time using a heap.

For ascending order, a max-heap repeatedly exposes the largest value at the root. Swap that root with the last unsorted position, shrink the heap boundary, and restore the max-heap property.

The key invariant is that the sorted suffix never needs to be touched again.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Heap Sort: apply the heap invariant and the correct array-index relationships for reliable implementation.

checkpoint.question: Why is heap sort O(N log N)?
options: It performs O(N) heap extractions, with each restoration taking O(log N).
It compares every pair of elements once.
It uses hashing for every element.
It always performs exactly N recursive splits.
checkpoint.explanation: After heap construction, each of the O(N) extractions requires O(log N) heap restoration.

pages.title: Kth largest number MCQ
pages.content:
### K-th Largest with a Heap
To find the K-th largest value, keep a **min-heap of size K**.

For each value, insert it. If the heap size exceeds `K`, remove its smallest value. After all values are processed, the root is the K-th largest value.

This gives `O(N log K)` time and `O(K)` extra space, and duplicate values count separately.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Kth largest number MCQ: apply the heap invariant and the correct array-index relationships for reliable implementation.

questions.question: In a min-heap, which value is guaranteed to be at the root?
questions.explanation: A min-heap places the minimum at the root.

questions.question: What is the left-child index of node i in a zero-indexed heap array?
questions.explanation: The left child is stored at 2*i+1.

questions.question: What is the parent index of a non-root node i?
questions.explanation: Integer division of (i-1) by 2 gives the parent index.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time of heap insertion?
questions.explanation: A new value may move up the height of the complete tree.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time of deleting the heap root?
questions.explanation: The replacement can sift down through O(log N) levels.

questions.question: What is the complexity of bottom-up heap construction?
questions.explanation: Bottom-up heapify is linear in the number of elements.

questions.question: Which structure is most suitable for repeatedly retrieving the smallest value?
options: Unordered linked list with no search
questions.explanation: A min-heap gives constant-time root access and logarithmic updates.

questions.question: For K-th largest using a size-K min-heap, what does the root represent after all values are processed?
questions.explanation: The heap contains the K largest values, so its minimum is the K-th largest overall.

questions.question: What is the key heap-sort invariant after placing an element at the end?
options: The sorted suffix contains the largest elements in final positions.
The whole array is already sorted.
The heap becomes a perfect binary tree.
questions.explanation: Each extracted maximum is fixed in the sorted suffix.

questions.question: Why are heaps useful for priority queues?
options: They efficiently support insertion and removal of a highest-priority item.
They keep all values fully sorted after every insertion.
They guarantee O(1) insertion for all priorities.
They require no storage for queued items.
questions.explanation: Heaps provide an efficient balance between priority access and updates.
